div.p: Context. Optimal management of invasive species should determine the interval between lethal-control operations that will sustain a desired population suppression at minimum cost. This requires an understanding of the species' rate of recruitment following control. These data are difficult to acquire for vertebrate carnivores such as the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), which are not readily trapped or observed.
Aims. To provide a long-term evaluation of the effects of 1080 poison baiting on the abundance and extent of movement of red foxes in a semiarid environment.

Methods. We used non-invasive DNA sampling of fox hairs in semi-arid Western Australia where the population was subject to two episodes of aerially delivered sodium fluoroacetate (1080) poison baits within 12 months. Sampling took place at ~45-day intervals and individual foxes were identified by genotyping eight microsatellite DNA markers and a genderspecific marker. Open-population and spatially explicit mark-recapture models were used to estimate the density, apparent survival and movements of foxes before and following baiting.

Key results. Following a severe reduction in density after baiting, fox density during the ensuing 12 months increased slowly (0.01 foxes km -2 month -1 ), such that density had only reached 22% of pre-baiting levels ~10 months after the initial baiting. Moreover, recovery was non-linear as population growth was negligible for 6 months, then exhibited a nine-fold increase 7-9 months after control, coincident with the dispersal of juveniles in autumn. Fox movements between recaptures were on average 470% greater after baiting than before, in line with expectations for low-density populations, suggesting that the probability of encountering baits during this period would be higher than before baiting.

Conclusions. Baiting with 1080 poison significantly reduced the density of foxes, and the low density was sustained for more than 6 months. Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting when at low densities.

Implications. Control programs in this region may be carried out at low frequency to suppress fox density to a fraction of unbaited levels. The intensity of follow-up baiting may also be adjusted downwards, to take account of an increased probability of bait encounter in more mobile foxes.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In Australia, the most significant pest of both livestock and native biodiversity is the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), which was introduced from the United Kingdom in the 1870s and is now distributed across the southern 75% of the continent (Saunders et al. 1995). The combined ecological and agricultural cost of foxes to the Australian economy was estimated to be AU $227.5 million a year (McLeod 2004). This has motivated concerted efforts to control foxes in Australia, and a wide range of lethal techniques are employed for this purpose (Baxter et al. 2008). Of these, baiting with 1080 poison (sodium fluoroacetate) is the most effective because uptake rate is high, large-scale distribution is simple, and the elusive nature of foxes makes more direct approaches, such as trapping and shooting, difficult (Thomson and Algar 2000;Thomson et al. 2000;Gentle et al. 2007). Nevertheless, control by baiting remains an expensive undertaking, and establishing the most cost-effective ways to implement control programs is an ongoing research priority (Saunders and McLeod 2007).

Mathematical models of optimal control of invasive species identify post-control recruitment from outside an area of control as a key parameter that must be estimated accurately because it determines the appropriate frequency of control (Chatterjee 1973;Hone 1999;Rushton et al. 2006). The rate of recruitment via immigration is intimately related to the movement capabilities and behaviours of pests (Levins 2006). Foxes are capable of extensive movement, and are often rapid colonisers of vacant habitats following population perturbations (Harris and Trewhella 1988;Kinnear et al. 1988;Allen and Sargeant 1993;Meek and Saunders 2000). There are numerous examples where despite control removing many foxes, indices of fox density, such as occurrences of footprints, have remained effectively constant because of apparently high immigration from outside the area of control (e.g. Harding et al. 2001;Baker and Harris 2006;Piggott et al. 2008). In other examples, however, post-control recruitment has been slower and associated with the immigration of dispersing juveniles rather than surplus adults from adjacent regions (Thomson et al. 2000). These variations in rates of recruitment are likely to reflect differences in the spatial scales of control relative to the extent of fox movements in those areas, as well as seasonal and regional differences in movement behaviour (Thomson et al. 2000;Saunders et al. 2010). Yet, the difficulty of directly monitoring changes in fox density, and the ambiguous results often derived from activity indices (Anderson 2001), has meant that few of these examples have provided clear understandings of the drivers of post-control recruitment (Thomson et al. 2000), nor provided quantitative estimates of fox-recruitment rates that could be incorporated into predictive models of optimal management. Instead, control periodicity in Australia is largely determined through trial and error, and intervals between episodes of poison baiting in Australia vary from as frequently as monthly (Greentree et al. 2000) to annually (Gentle et al. 2007).

The extent of movement also determines the probability that invasive species will encounter poison baits or other control measures, and therefore dictates the optimal baiting density (Tompkins and Ramsey 2007;Moseby et al. 2009;Saunders et al. 2010). Although there have been numerous investigations of fox movement in Australia and elsewhere (Coman 1988), and it is generally appreciated that movement is a dynamic characteristic of fox behaviour that changes in response to population density (Trewhella et al. 1988), there have been few published manipulative experiments where both density and movements have been measured (Frey and Conover 2007;Iossa et al. 2009;Moseby et al. 2009). This limits the capacity of managers to optimise control strategically according to the characteristics of focal populations, and in practice, the intensity of fox baiting in Australia ranges from 5 baits km -2 to 50 baits km -2 (Thomson et al. 2000;Algar and Burrows 2004;Saunders et al. 2010).

Non-invasive genetic techniques ('genetic tagging') have recently been employed to characterise aspects of fox populations in Australia (Piggott et al. 2008;Vine et al. 2009;Berry et al. 2012) and have been employed to great effect elsewhere for similarly elusive carnivores (Woods et al. 1999;Lucchini et al. 2002). By permitting individuals to be identified, they enable mark-recapture modelling of key population parameters such as density and survival. Few non-invasive DNA studies have examined dynamic aspects of invasive species populations, such as changes in density in response to population perturbations or changes to the spatial ecology of pests (but see Prugh et al. 2005;Marucco et al. 2009). Here, we use non-invasively collected hair samples from a red fox population subject to lethal control and apply mark-recapture modelling to generate one of the first quantitative estimates of the rate of population recovery in a fox population in Australia subject to control with 1080 poison. We also investigate changes in the extent of movement by foxes before and after control.

div.head: Study site
div.p: Details on the study site have been presented elsewhere (see Berry et al. 2012), and a brief summary is presented here. The study was carried out at Karara and Lochada pastoral stations, Western Australia (28 58 0 05 00 S, 116 40 0 51 00 E), which are adjacent reclaimed pastoral leases. The landscape is semiarid (rainfall 320 mm annually) and is dominated by mixed Acacia shrublands and sparse York gum (Eucalyptus loxophleba) woodlands. Minimal predator control had been conducted on the pastoral leases and the surrounding area before the present study and mostly by neighbouring pastoral leases in an ad hoc manner, to control wild dogs (Canis familiaris).

div.head: Sampling
div.p: We employed eight transects, each containing 11 'sticky wicket' hair-snares spaced at 1-km intervals. The 'sticky wicket' trapped hair as foxes passed between three vertical sticks covered in double-sided tape to enter a monitoring plot containing scent and audio lures (Berry et al. 2012). We employed a mixture of linear and irregularly shaped transects that encompassed 90degree bends. By necessity, transects ran along dirt tracks and hair-snares were placed adjacent and running perpendicular to the tracks within the shrubland vegetation. Although the tracks were predominantly cleared of vegetation, in general, the dominant shrubland vegetation at Karara-Lochada is open enough that foxes can travel unimpeded. We, therefore, assumed that the placement of hair-snares in the vicinity of the tracks minimally biased our analysis. Furthermore, the even density of tracks throughout Karara-Lochada (Fig. 1) should mean that our analysis was representative of the study area. The present study incorporated capture information from the final two sessions reported previously (Berry et al. 2012), namely June and August 2008, here identified as Sessions 1 and 2, and extended an identical sampling regime of ~45-day intervals between sampling sessions that each consisted of four consecutive sampling days (occasions) for a further 12 months until July 2009 (six further sessions). The final sampling session in July 2009 occurred 20 days after deployment from an aircraft of 1080 poison baits at 50 baits km -2 , which was identical to the deployment implemented in August 2008 (Berry et al. 2012), and covered the entire Karara-Lochada study site and a further 5-km buffer from the property boundary. Fifty baits km -2 is the operational rate for feral-cat control (Algar and Burrows 2004). A large rainfall event followed several days after the September 2008 baiting, making it unlikely that baits remained viable for long after. In total, eight sampling sessions took place; however, samples were not obtained for three of these sessions because foxes were absent or at extremely low densities and hairs were not collected on hair-snares.

Sticky wickets were checked daily and hairs were removed from the tape with sterilised forceps, placed in a sealed paper envelope, labelled, frozen at À20 C and transported to the DNA laboratory within 2 weeks of collection. To limit any effect of time on the quality and quantity of DNA in each follicle, DNA extraction was carried out within 2 weeks of the receipt of the samples. Laboratory analyses were conducted under strict protocols and guidelines, to minimise poor-quality samples and reduce genotyping errors (see Berry et al. (2012). DNA was extracted from a maximum of 10 hairs per sample (minimum 1; mean 3.8 AE 0.2) by using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Cat. 69504; Hilden, Germany).

div.head: Genotyping and individual identification
div.p: Following DNA extraction, samples were genotyped with eight microsatellite DNA loci and the gender of each fox was determined with a male-specific sry product (Berry et al. 2012). Three PCR replicates of each locus were made for each sample. Results of the fragment analysis were analysed using GENEMARKER (SoftGenetics, State College, PA, USA) and all allele calling was checked by eye. The male-specific marker amplified only in the presence of male fox DNA. Therefore, to distinguish between a female and failed amplification, each sample without sry amplification was cross-referenced, with the amplification success of two microsatellite loci coamplified in the PCR multiplex (Berry et al. 2012).

Consensus genotypes were calculated according to the criterion of Frantz et al. (2003) where a homozygous genotype was accepted if the same single allele was present in all three replicates, and a heterozygous genotype was accepted if two different alleles were present in each of two or more replicates. Consensus genotypes for each sample were input into the Excel macro GENECAP (Wilberg and Dreher 2004), which identified genotypes differing by one or two alleles, generated capture histories, provided allele frequencies and probability of identity (PID) statistics (Waits et al. 2001). On the basis of PID results presented in Berry et al. (2012), samples that produced consensus genotypes at five or more loci were sufficiently informative to distinguish individuals and were used to create capture histories. Samples that did not meet the criteria were re-amplified and re-genotyped to obtain more complete genotypes (one example in each of Sessions 1 and 2). Allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed from the data with the program GIMLET (Valiere 2002). Identifying individual foxes in this manner is analogous to direct capture for the purposes of capture-recapture analysis.

div.head: Density estimation using spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) models
div.p: Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) models generated in the program DENSITY were used to estimate the density of foxes within Sessions 1, 6 and 7 (Efford 2004;Efford et al. 2009). SECR uses the locations that each animal is captured to fit a model of the detection process and to provide an estimate of density that is unbiased by incomplete detection and edge effects (Efford 2004). We used the full maximum likelihood estimator (Borchers and Efford 2008) of density (D), and a halfnormal detection function incorporating g 0 (susceptibility to capture at the centre of a home range), and s (a measure of the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture). We identified our hair-snares as proximity detectors (allowing multiple withinoccasion captures per individual), and ran the analysis with a buffer of 10 000 m. Alternative buffer sizes and detection functions had a minimal effect on parameter estimates. Sixteen biologically plausible models were fitted to the capture data and their fit was evaluated with Akaike's information criterion corrected for a small sample size (AICc; Burnham and Anderson 2002). We tested models that maintained a constant density throughout the sampling period, D(.), or a change in density between sessions, D(session). Models that allowed for behavioural responses to capture (b), and individual heterogeneity (two-group mixture; h), in both g 0 and s, and all combinations of these variables, were also tested. Parameters were estimated with model averaging. Sessions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 were excluded from the SECR analyses because, at most, one sample was collected in any of those sessions. However, an approximate density was calculated for Sessions 2 and 5 when a single fox was captured by dividing one by the mean effective sampling area identified with SECR modelling during three pre-baiting sessions (Berry et al. 2012;293.3 km 2 ). Sex was not included in the models because of low sample sizes.

div.head: Apparent survival and abundance
div.p: Open-population capture-recapture analysis, based on Pollock's robust design, was conducted with the program MARK (White and Burnham 1999). This analysis enabled estimation of apparent survival (s), capture probability (p), recapture probability (c), abundance ( N ) and temporary immigration (G). Four biologically plausible models were constructed that included behavioural responses to capture (probability of recapture = probability of capture) and individual heterogeneity in capture (two-group mixture). Models that incorporated change in survival and abundance between sessions were also considered, as were models that kept these parameters constant. This analysis was applied to all sessions where foxes were detected (i.e. excluding Sessions 3, 4 and 8). The support for competing models was ranked with AICc, and parameters were estimated with model averaging.

div.head: Movement between recaptures
div.p: The mean distance moved by individual foxes between recaptures was calculated as the cumulative distance moved between trapping locations in order of recapture date within a session, divided by the number of recaptures. Individuals never recaptured were not included in these analyses. For this analysis, we included movement information from foxes collected under comparable experimental conditions during pre-baiting Sessions 1-3 described in Berry et al. (2012). Data were checked for homogeneity of variances with Cochran's C test. Data with heterogeneous variances were log-transformed. A Student's t-test comparing the log10 mean distance moved before and after 1080 baiting (Sessions 2-7) was conducted with the software package JMP (version 5.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

div.head: Species identification, genotyping and error rates
div.p: Thirty-five hair samples were collected during Sessions 3-8. These were added to the 52 samples collected from Sessions 1 and 2 that represented 24 individual foxes (Berry et al. 2012).

Thirty-four of the 35 samples were identified as fox, and of these, 33 (97%) provided more than five locus microsatellite genotypes (6 locus n = 2, 8 locus n = 31; Table S1, available as Supplementary Material for this paper). Including the samples from Sessions 1 and 2, 60, 21 and four samples provided eight, seven and six locus genotypes, respectively (no five locus genotypes). No samples contained more than two alleles at any loci, indicating that there were no instances of mixed samples.

Comparisons of genotypes revealed no cases of one-and twoallele mismatches. The average per locus, per replicate rate of allelic dropout (ADO) was 0.016, and the average per locus, per replicate rate of false alleles (FA) was 0.014. The probability of identity (sibling) for the most variable five loci was 0.006, and for the five least variable loci was 0.012, indicating that the fivelocus criterion for accepting genotypes was acceptable. The probability of identity (unrelated) for both the most and least variable five loci was <0.001. Among samples identified as recaptures, the mean probability that any pair of samples were full siblings rather than true recaptures (PIDsib) was 0.003 (AE0.0002 s.e.) and the maximum PIDsib between any pair of samples was 0.012, with only one instance of >0.01

div.head: Fox capture histories
div.p: Five samples (15%) collected during Sessions 3-8 yielded unique genotypes, and thus represented individual foxes. Twenty-eight samples (85%) yielded genotypes that were present at least twice in the dataset and represented six different individuals. In total, 11 individual foxes (seven males and four females) were identified during Sessions 2-7. The initial pre-baiting (Session 1) sex ratio of male:female was 1 : 1.3 (n = 23) and post-baiting (Sessions 2-8) was 1.75 : 1 (n = 11).

The sex ratio pre and post-baiting was not significantly different (c 2 with Yates correction = 0.54, P = 0.46). None of the 23 foxes caught in the session before baiting was recaptured in any of the seven sessions following baiting.

div.head: Density
div.p: Density was estimated directly for Sessions 1, 6 and 7, when multiple individual foxes were detected. All well supported models incorporated a session effect on density and the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture (s) (Table 1). The best supported model also included a behavioural response to capture (probability of capture = probability of recapture), and heterogeneity in response to capture g 0 (b + h). Models ranked 2 and 3 also included heterogeneity in s. The parameter estimates for Session 1 differ slightly from those from the same session (labelled Session 3) in Berry et al. (2012) because of differences in the models selected by AICc and the incorporation of data from different sessions.

Fox density decreased substantially following the initial 1080 baiting, from an estimate of 0.51 foxes km -2 (AE0.17 s.e.) to 0.003 foxes km -2 . Over the following 12 months (7 sessions) density remained very low and not estimatable by SECR, until Sessions 6 and 7 when it increased to a maximum of 0.11 foxes km -2 AE 0.04 s.e. just before the second episode of aerial baiting (Fig. 2), after which no foxes were detected in Session 8. The probability of capture at the centre of a home range g 0 was 0.160 (AE0.092 s.e.) and 0.007 (AE0.014 s.e.) for the 'trap happy' and 'trap shy' groups, respectively.

div.head: Abundance and apparent survival
div.p: The best supported model incorporated change in abundance and apparent survival between sessions and assumed unequal probability of capture and recapture (Table 2). Temporary emigration was constant in these models. Model averaging indicated that there were 30.75 trappable foxes (AE6.83 s.e.) present at Karara-Lochada during Session 1 before the initial baiting and 3.23 (AE0.079 s.e.) in Session 2 immediately after baiting and also in Session 5 (Fig. 3). Ten months after baiting, the number of trappable foxes present in the study area had risen to 12.94 (AE4.09 s.e.) by Session 7. The model-averaged probability of capture was 0.20 (AE0.07 s.e.), and probability of recapture was 0.23 (AE0.04 s.e.). Apparent survival following the initial 1080 baiting (between Sessions 1 and 2) was effectively zero, and remained zero (inestimable) for ~7 months because of zero or sparse captures until the period between Sessions 6 and 7, where it rose to 0.68, which is similar to that before baiting (Berry et al. 2012), although the analysis could not resolve standard error for this estimate because of limited sample size.

div.head: Changes in the extent of movement between recaptures
div.p: Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting than they did before baiting (Fig. 4; t = 3.41, d.f. = 18, Table 1. Models fitted for spatially explicit capture-recapture analysis of fox density at Karara-Lochada Station, Western Australia, during three sampling sessions, namely Session 1 (prebait), Session 6 and Session 7 (post-bait) Models are defined in terms of whether density was constant (.) or varied between sessions (session), and the effects of behaviour (b) and individual heterogeneity (h) on g 0 and s, and whether s differed between sessions (session). P < 0.001). Individual foxes did not move between transects in the pre-baiting session, but three foxes moved between transects following baiting, with two of these foxes (both male) moving over 10 km in one day. The parameter s, which describes the spatial extent in susceptibility of capture, and thus indexes home-range size (Efford 2004), was 629.01 m (AE119.52 s.e.) in Session 1 before baiting. During Sessions 6 and 7 (when captures were sufficient to estimate s), it increased to 5174.74 m (AE1078.26 s.e.) and 2600.64 m (AE834.62 s.e.), respectively (values from the best supported model).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: There is clear evidence that 1080 poison baiting can reduce the abundance of red foxes and their impacts on Australian native species (Kinnear et al. 1988). Yet, it is commonly recognised that even when control induces high mortality in fox populations, rapid re-invasion can limit its effectiveness or even nullify it altogether (Gentle et al. 2007;Piggott et al. 2008). This, together with the logistical difficulties of conducting control over appropriately large regions, has led to pessimism about the long-term cost-effectiveness of existing approaches to baiting in Australia (Saunders et al. 2010). However, not all instances of fox control are followed by immediate re-invasion. Our results mirror those of Thomson et al. (2000) in Australia, and several studies from the United Kingdom (Lloyd 1980), demonstrating both slow, and irregular re-invasion after control. Identifying the factors that dictate the pace of recruitment in fox populations and explain widely contrasting recruitment dynamics should provide opportunities to improve the effectiveness of control by better aligning it with fox ecology. Historically, the dynamics of fox populations in response to control have relied on activity indices and been difficult to monitor with confidence (Saunders et al. 1995). Recent investigations incorporating genetic tagging have significantly improved the resolution of fox-population monitoring by enabling individuals to be identified and facilitating robust mark-recapture estimation of key population parameters (Piggott et al. 2008;Berry et al. 2012). Here, this approach has permitted the first long-term quantitative account of change in the density of a fox population as it recovers from a severe population reduction induced by 1080 poison baiting. We have demonstrated a sustained reduction of fox density following control, such that the density of foxes 10 months after the initial round of baiting in August 2008 was only 21.6% of the pre-baiting estimate. This corresponds to the remarkably low rate of recruitment of ~0.01 foxes recruiting per square kilometre per month. However, the true rate was much lower for close to 7 months following the initial baiting before rapidly increasing by Session 6 in April 2009. Although we could not record the ages of foxes, it is likely that the rapid increase at this time reflected the dispersal of juvenile animals born outside the baited area in the previous year, because this pattern of annual movement by juveniles is typically observed in red foxes (Saunders et al. 1995).

Slow post-control recruitment contrasts strongly with most instances of fox control in mesic parts of Australia where reinvasion has been almost immediate (Rushton et al. 2006;Piggott et al. 2008). Paradoxically, foxes at low densities are more mobile than those at high densities (Trewhella et al. 1988), and should therefore have high capacity to invade vacant territories, especially considering the absence of physical barriers. The established relationships between fox dispersal and density (Trewhella et al. 1988) suggest that a 5-km buffer of baits outside of the study site could be readily traversed by dispersing foxes. Thomson et al. (2000) also noted that most post-control recruits in an arid zone fox population arrived during autumn and that this coincided with the typical juveniledispersal phase of foxes, but did not discuss why this differed so significantly from populations inhabiting mesic environments. However, they did recognise that the seasonality of dispersal in foxes offers opportunities to strategically focus baiting during this phase (Thomson et al. 2000).

If, as appears likely, dispersal by juvenile foxes drove the re-invasion of vacant territory at Karara-Lochada, what prevented adult foxes from exploiting this vacant habitat earlier? A plausible explanation lies in interplay between fox social behaviour and the availability of resources at Karara-Lochada. Adult foxes generally defend exclusive territories (Macdonald 1977), and at Karara-Lochada, a significant fraction of the population show strong site fidelity and very limited movements, indicating that they are territorial adults (Berry et al. 2012). Within territories, however, foxes exhibit highly varied social structures, largely reflecting the availability of resources (Cavallini 1996). High-density populations inhabiting resource-rich environments typically retain non-reproductive 'helpers' within territories (Macdonald 1979;Zabel and Taggart 1989;Iossa et al. 2009). These individuals trade immediate reproductive opportunities for future access to parental or neighbouring territories (Macdonald 1979). In contrast, low-density populations inhabiting resource-poor environments typically exist as monogamous pairs (Storm et al. 1976). The fate of nonterritorial foxes in landscapes where monogamy is predominant is not well studied, but their survival at Karara-Lochada is low (Berry et al. 2012). The presence or absence of non-reproductive 'surplus' individuals within resource-rich and resource-poor landscapes, respectively, could significantly influence the available pool of immigrants, and explain the contrasting post-control recruitment dynamics. The frequency of non-reproductive foxes observed in high-and low-density Australian fox population is consistent with this suggestion (Marlow et al. 2000;McIlroy et al. 2001;Saunders et al. 2002). It follows that distinct mechanisms may drive recruitment in these contrasting landscapes; post-control recruitment in low-density fox populations may largely be driven by juvenile recruitment during their seasonal dispersive phase as observed here and by Thomson et al. (2000), whereas in high-density populations, it may also be driven by opportunism in 'surplus' animals. These alternative mechanisms of re-invasion require further investigation, including a better understanding of the age and social status of re-invading foxes in resourcerich environments. However, if the alternative mechanisms are supported, they imply that successful fox-control programs may require different strategies regionally in terms of timing and frequency of control, and on the basis of understanding of density, social organisation and their relationship to movement. Also requiring explanation is the failure of neighbouring reproductive territory holders to expand their territories to incorporate the vacant habitat at Karara-Lochada. Territory expansion following the demise of neighbours has been observed in foxes from the northern hemisphere (Sargeant 1972;Baker et al. 2000). A leading explanation for what motivates animals to disperse is to avoid competition for resources (Clobert et al. 2001). The failure of territory holders to expand their territories could indicate that resources are not sufficiently limited within their existing territories (see Englund 1980;Lloyd 1980;Bino et al. 2010), or the converse, that territory expansion is too costly in such a resource-poor environment. Alternatively, the 5-km-wide buffer zone surrounding the baited area may have been sufficient to absorb territory increases.

Once post-baiting recruitment did commence, we documented a pronounced increase in the extent of movement in foxes compared with those recorded before baiting. This is consistent with the expectation that foxes are more mobile at lower population densities (Trewhella et al. 1988;Baker et al. 2000), and it suggests that the absence of recruits immediately post-control was unlikely to be the result of incapacity to disperse across the buffer zone. Of the recolonising foxes in the present study, two moved particularly large distances (>10 km in one day) and three were recaptured on different transects. In contrast, inter-transect movement was never documented before baiting, and the mean distance moved between recaptures over the course of 6 months was 1178 m (Berry et al. 2012).

This increased mobility of recolonising foxes implies that the optimal intensity of follow-up baiting may be less than the initial intensity because the likelihood of foxes encountering poison baits should increase. According to the bait-detection relationship described by Moseby and Read (2006), follow-up baiting programs could reduce the density of baits by close to 80% without reducing their effectiveness. However, this assumes that the foraging behaviour of re-invading foxes is equivalent to foxes in non-controlled landscapes (see Arthur et al. 2002), and this has not been investigated.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: The resilience of fox populations to control operations depends in part on their capacity to recruit from outside controlled sites. Foxes at Karara-Lochada exhibited a much slower rate of post-control re-invasion than has been observed in almost all accounts of fox control from Australia. The explanations for this anomaly are unclear, but we hypothesise that it reflects an absence of non-reproductive 'helper' foxes in this resource-poor region. Fox populations in these environments may be effectively recruit-limited for long periods. Assuming our findings are general for arid-zone fox populations rather than a site-specific anomaly, they have several implications for the effectiveness of poison baiting at the Karara-Lochada site and elsewhere. First, follow-up baiting in this region could be conducted at low frequency and still maintain low fox densities. Second, in regions where fox densities are low and dominated by monogamous pairs, strategically baiting during the dispersal phase of juvenile foxes may be as effective as baiting more frequently throughout the year. Finally, follow-up baiting may be conducted at lower intensities to account for the increased probability of bait encounter in more mobile re-invading foxes. The generality of the results presented here should be tested with additional studies of arid-zone fox populations.
